newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung modifies planned civil liberties curbs.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung modifies planned civil liberties curbs.

text.p: Hong Kong's future government on Thursday announced changes to planned civil liberties curbs that it plans to impose when the British colony reverts to China on July 1, but the basic principles remained unaltered.
At a news conference, Michael Suen, an aide to leader-to-be Tung Chee-hwa, unveiled a diluted version of curbs on protests and a modified ban on foreign funding of local political groups.

Suen said revisions were made after digesting the public's views during a three-week pulse-taking exercise, which has been marked by virulent opposition from the pro-democracy camp to any rollback of political freedoms.

He said stringent prior notification rules for protest marches had been dropped and that the foreign funding ban would now only bar funding of local groups by foreign political organisations, not by individual benefactors.

Existing arrangements on protest marches would be kept. The original curbs plan required notification to the police not less than seven days before a protest, with discretion for police to accept late notification up to two days beforehand. "But having considered all views expressed on this subject, the Executive Council of the (future) government has decided to cancel this particular suggestion," Suen said.

He said Tung's cabinet also dropped the "protection of public health and morals" as a reason for banning a protest. But "national security" would be kept as a reason for a ban and was defined as the "safeguarding of China's territorial integrity and independence", which as widely expected will outlaw protests advocating independence for Taiwan and Tibet.
